original_before_fields.stance: Doyle treats affordable bread as a moral and political expectation whose repeated frustration shaped popular allegiance; scarcity is a continuing thread, not a series of unrelated episodes.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Economic and subsistence crisis, 1788-1789
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The interacting harvest failure, severe winter, high bread prices, falling consumption, unemployment, and popular distress that formed the material setting of the political crisis. Popular attribution of hardship to government and its commercial choices made economic suffering politically consequential. Interlocking harvest, price, employment, and consumption shocks formed the material setting in which constitutional conflict became volatile. Hail, drought, and the exceptionally severe winter of 1788-1789 damaged crops and transport across much of France. Escalating grain, flour, and bread prices absorbed extraordinary shares of working people's income and repeatedly generated fear and disorder. Working people associated grain policy, commercial policy, scarcity, and unemployment with governmental failure.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The chapter treats economic misery as an acute, nationwide intensifier of political tension, not as a sufficient standalone cause of revolution. Distinguish interacting material causes from contemporary blame; do not infer the treaty’s full economic effect from the short time it had operated or collapse the differing price-peak comparisons into one statistic. The chapter treats economic distress as a powerful condition and accelerator of political change, not as a sufficient single-cause explanation. Weather is presented as a nationwide material shock that worsened an already unstable economy. The chapter makes subsistence pressure a continuing bridge between economic distress, public mobilization, and the July uprising. The chapter treats these perceptions as politically consequential even where the causal attribution was overstated.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Bread scarcity and popular mobilization in 1789
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Continuing urban and rural bread scarcity linked subsistence to revolutionary politics throughout 1789. In autumn, dry weather, milling and supply difficulties, convoy protests, troop arrival and reports of cockade insults revived conspiracy fears and mobilized Parisian women. High prices, uncertain supply, and hunger rumours repeatedly transform economic distress into revolutionary mobilization in Paris, towns, and the countryside. The summoning of troops and reports of an anti-patriotic royal banquet recreated the perceived military and starvation threat that had preceded July.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Distinguish material shortage and administrative disruption from unproved intentional starvation plots. Women initiated the October mobilization, while earlier subsistence interventions had broader urban and rural participants. The author emphasizes the interaction of real shortages, natural and administrative disruptions, and politically charged conspiracy beliefs. The author distinguishes rumours and symbolism from the real political effect of a renewed coercive threat amid bread scarcity.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Versailles concentrated rank, costly display, royal rewards and privileged access in a court system that made nobles dependent on favour while giving courtiers influence over wealth and appointments. Louis XIV’s court domestication remained an inheritance, modified by eighteenth-century noble recovery of major offices; successive favourites and ministers illustrate the operation of patronage. Versailles consumed major revenue, supported a dependent town and palace population, ranked courtiers by ancestry and presentation, and concentrated the kingdom's wealthiest, most influential noble elite. Royal favor allocated pensions, sinecures, office, and influence; favorites and mistresses could enrich families and make or break ministers. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV’s favouritism and mistresses influenced ministerial careers and court patronage. Louis XIV’s domestication of nobles at court supplied a baseline later altered by noble recovery of elite government.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Distinguish the patronage system from territorial expansion, army development and judicial sovereignty. Examples of favourites explain access and influence, not a claim that all government was reducible to mistresses. Preserve both relatively open physical access and highly exclusive true court status. Do not dismiss court intrigue as trivial: the memoir details concerned real wealth and power. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. Louis XV had failed to prepare his heir; the young queen and court appointment pressures formed the immediate setting of the new reign. The twenty-year-old king was educated, devout, dutiful, and well-intentioned but poorly prepared, insecure, unimpressive, and unlikely to master the intrigue surrounding the throne. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV failed to prepare his heir for kingship; this shaped the personal inheritance at accession. Louis XVI’s indecisive accession contrasted with Louis XIV’s decisive assumption of authority.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Credit conscientious intentions while retaining political insecurity. Early marital and court tensions do not establish later revolutionary accusations; territorial conquest and army history belong to their own requirements. Avoid caricature: credit good intentions and duty while preserving the author's judgment of inadequate political mastery. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Marie Antoinette, the Diamond Necklace affair, and court disrepute
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Sexual and political pamphleteering, hostility to Austrian influence, and the Diamond Necklace affair made Marie Antoinette a focal point for distrust of the Court. Early accession hopes and ridicule of the royal marriage gave way to relatively improved esteem for the king, while hostility to the queen and court persisted. The 1787 disclosure of taxpayer costs reinforced discredit. The alliance with France's traditional Austrian enemy remained unpopular, and its renewal through the heir's marriage to Marie Antoinette was marred by a fatal Paris crowd disaster interpreted as an omen. The new king initially carried hopes for a clean break with Louis XV, but failure to produce an heir and his private marital difficulties quickly became material for corrosive public pamphleteering. The queen's Austrian identity, spending, favorites, political interventions, and family diplomacy made her a persuasive target for rumor and hostility even when specific accusations were false. Although Marie Antoinette was uninvolved in the necklace swindle, Rohan's public trial, acquittal, celebration, and subsequent exile confirmed damaging assumptions about her conduct and deepened hostility to the court. The necklace scandal returned the court to the disrepute of Louis XV's final years, and the first disclosure of its cost to taxpayers in 1787 reinforced the political damage.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The queen was not involved in the necklace fraud, but Rohan's acquittal and the royal response enabled the scandal to damage her and deepen public disrepute of court society. Separate initial alliance hostility, actual indiscretions and false accusations in the Necklace fraud; later fiscal disclosure reinforced reputation damage rather than being the sole cause of financial crisis. Do not project all later hostility to the queen backward; the passage identifies an early diplomatic and symbolic burden. Preserve the contrast between initial confidence and later ridicule without treating reproductive satire as a complete measure of royal legitimacy. Distinguish documented indiscretion and unpopularity from fabricated responsibility for the necklace fraud. State the queen's noninvolvement clearly while preserving the affair's reputational and political consequences. Do not claim court expenditure alone caused the fiscal crisis; its importance here is reputational and symbolic.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Versailles concentrated rank, costly display, royal rewards and privileged access in a court system that made nobles dependent on favour while giving courtiers influence over wealth and appointments. Louis XIV’s court domestication remained an inheritance, modified by eighteenth-century noble recovery of major offices; successive favourites and ministers illustrate the operation of patronage. Versailles consumed major revenue, supported a dependent town and palace population, ranked courtiers by ancestry and presentation, and concentrated the kingdom's wealthiest, most influential noble elite. Royal favor allocated pensions, sinecures, office, and influence; favorites and mistresses could enrich families and make or break ministers. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV’s favouritism and mistresses influenced ministerial careers and court patronage. Louis XIV’s domestication of nobles at court supplied a baseline later altered by noble recovery of elite government.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Distinguish the patronage system from territorial expansion, army development and judicial sovereignty. Examples of favourites explain access and influence, not a claim that all government was reducible to mistresses. Preserve both relatively open physical access and highly exclusive true court status. Do not dismiss court intrigue as trivial: the memoir details concerned real wealth and power. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. Louis XV had failed to prepare his heir; the young queen and court appointment pressures formed the immediate setting of the new reign. The twenty-year-old king was educated, devout, dutiful, and well-intentioned but poorly prepared, insecure, unimpressive, and unlikely to master the intrigue surrounding the throne. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV failed to prepare his heir for kingship; this shaped the personal inheritance at accession. Louis XVI’s indecisive accession contrasted with Louis XIV’s decisive assumption of authority.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Credit conscientious intentions while retaining political insecurity. Early marital and court tensions do not establish later revolutionary accusations; territorial conquest and army history belong to their own requirements. Avoid caricature: credit good intentions and duty while preserving the author's judgment of inadequate political mastery. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

exact_destination_scopes.label: France—territorial composition and enclaves
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The kingdom accumulated territories through conquest and dynastic inheritance, leaving enclaves, uneven provincial identities and boundaries rather than a uniformly planned territory. Its population scale formed the setting for this inherited composition. The monarchy governed a large, growing realm assembled by conquest and dynastic acquisition, still containing papal, German, and municipal enclaves. The kingdom’s large and increasing population forms background to its composite territory.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The territorial picture reflects historical accumulation; later demographic pressure, urban growth and the bourgeoisie’s relative expansion are separate social arguments. Do not treat territorial irregularity as anomalous to contemporaries; it was established by law and prescription.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Poverty—scale, causes, and demographic pressure
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Chronic underemployment, family dependency, population growth, and wages lagging prices left roughly a third of the population poor even in good times. Roughly a third of the population lacked secure support even in good times, with millions more vulnerable when crops or jobs failed; population growth expanded able-bodied underemployment. Prices rose much faster than wages, so marriage, children, illness, or harvest failure could move working families from subsistence into beggary. Population growth and predominantly rural settlement intensified pressure on employment, food and relief institutions.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Poverty is presented as a structural failure of the economy to provide secure livelihoods, not mainly a moral failure of the poor. Explain poverty structurally rather than as moral failure. Treat family formation as exposing inadequate earnings, not causing poverty through moral irresponsibility.
exact_destination_scopes.scope: Use only this coherent parent’s actual temporal/causal scope; no wholesale replication of a broad historical unit under every destination.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Urbanization—rural connections and uneven town growth
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Markets, cottage industry, labor migration, and demographic inflow bound towns to villages, while commercial centers grew much faster than bypassed provincial towns. Food purchases, market towns, cottage-industry organization, product marketing, and migration tied most rural households closely to towns. The urban share rose through rural immigration and rapid growth in major commercial cities, while towns bypassed by expansion stagnated. Urban growth coexisted with predominance of small towns and a largely rural population.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The urban-rural boundary was porous; growth concentrated wealth, literacy, and dynamism without eliminating widespread urban poverty. Reject a simple town-country divide while preserving distinct settlement patterns. Preserve the coexistence of dynamic cities, small agrarian towns, and stagnant provincial centers.

exact_destination_scopes.label: France—legal, fiscal, and commercial fragmentation
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Customary and Roman law, weights and measures, direct taxes, the gabelle, tolls, and internal customs varied sharply by locality. Written Roman law in much of the south and numerous northern customs produced district-level differences in marriage, inheritance, and property tenure. Direct and salt taxation varied sharply by province, tax base, and privilege, with northern and central France generally bearing heavier burdens. Nonuniform weights and measures and dense internal excise, toll, tariff, and customs barriers obstructed exchange and encouraged litigation and fraud fears.

exact_destination_scopes.label: France—legal, fiscal, and commercial fragmentation
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Customary and Roman law, weights and measures, direct taxes, the gabelle, tolls, and internal customs varied sharply by locality. Written Roman law in much of the south and numerous northern customs produced district-level differences in marriage, inheritance, and property tenure. Direct and salt taxation varied sharply by province, tax base, and privilege, with northern and central France generally bearing heavier burdens. Nonuniform weights and measures and dense internal excise, toll, tariff, and customs barriers obstructed exchange and encouraged litigation and fraud fears.

exact_destination_scopes.label: French agriculture—low productivity and fragmented peasant property
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Conservative technology, partible inheritance, morcellation, small ownership, and piecemeal leasing constrained productivity and marketable surplus. French farming was generally low-yield, conservative, and wasteful, and government-backed agrarian improvement discourse had little effect on ordinary practice. Partible inheritance repeatedly divided property, producing morcellation, small estates, and obstacles to compact management and capital-intensive farming. Millions of small owner-occupiers and widespread sharecropping organized cultivation in tiny, precarious units whose uncertain yields discouraged fixed rent.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The author broadly accepts contemporary diagnoses of backwardness but explains the rational pressures behind small-scale cultivation and sharecropping. Treat backwardness as structural and uneven, not simply peasant ignorance or indolence. Treat legal inheritance as a root mechanism, while recognizing Church land as an exception. Present ownership and métayage as distinct tenure forms sharing small scale and insecurity.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Page 15 supplies a coherent major requirement: deteriorating traditional support, mortmain restrictions, debt/inflation losses, and limited Masonic, philanthropic and governmental experiments amid public concern. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Express the principal reasons for declining resources in the parent meaning. Retain p. 15 public debate, and rehome the broad opinion examples on pp. 9/23/35/37/38. Broader print infrastructure may be contextual, but it should not create an independent relief demand.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 22–23 sustain the essential requirement for bourgeois numerical growth, wealth, consumption and cultural patronage, with internal diversity and non-inevitability of revolution preserved. The full old public-opinion dossier was also copied into this subject. Government agricultural debate, parliamentary remonstrances and the Maupeou propaganda failure are not established on pp. 9/37/38 as bourgeois wealth or patronage. The source explicitly treats multiple institutional actors.
prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Retain the wealth/cultural/inequality requirement and the p. 23 print infrastructure. Do not infer bourgeois authorship from educated public debate.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 34–35 directly support Brienne’s reform/political career, Jesuit expulsion, utilitarian criticism and selective dissolution which spared large institutions and unresolved parish problems. Those are separate source treatments, not evidence of Jesuit/monastic reform.
prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Keep reform-relevant p. 35 opinion and p. 34 Brienne context. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 37–38 accurately explain appellate/administrative powers, registration and remonstrance, publicity and obstruction, fiscal confrontation and ultimate royal authority. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 38–39 support Maupeou’s coercive yet rationalizing reform, cooperation by some magistrates, failed legitimacy, restoration and durable damage to both Crown and courts. exact_destination_scopes.label: Poor relief—ecclesiastical decline and public innovation
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Traditional alms, hospitals and poor houses lost resources through restrictions on mortmain acquisition, weakened bequests, government debt measures and inflation. Lay philanthropy, masonic charity, depots de mendicite and charitable workshops tentatively supplemented ecclesiastical relief. Urban monasteries, hospitals, poorhouses, and private charity attracted migrants but became increasingly inadequate as claims grew and resources eroded. Masonic charity, philanthropic societies, dépôts de mendicité, and ateliers de charité represented tentative new lay and governmental responses to a feared crisis. Press, literary circles, learned societies and academies debated the crisis of poverty.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Public concern and innovation grew, but resources remained inadequate to the scale of poverty. Wider agricultural, judicial and Church controversies are not independent obligations of this welfare requirement. Do not portray traditional provision as comprehensive even before its financial decline. Treat these as limited experiments rather than a national welfare system.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Bourgeoisie—growth, wealth, consumption, and culture
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled commercial, industrial, landed, officeholding and financial wealth. Its demand sustained urban building, luxury trades, education, theatres, print, reading rooms and associations; enrichment alongside growing poverty made inequality more visible. The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled much commercial, industrial, landed, office, and financial wealth, forming most of the secure urban elite. Bourgeois demand sustained luxury trades, theatres, schools, colleges, books, newspapers, libraries, reading rooms, clubs, and cultural societies. Simultaneous growth of mass poverty and elite wealth made luxury more visible and sharpened resentment between secure elites and precarious majorities. Books, newspapers, reading rooms, clubs and cultural societies expanded the social infrastructure of bourgeois cultural life.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: This internally unequal group was more than industrial entrepreneurs. Cultural resources and print demand do not demonstrate unified revolutionary politics or bourgeois authorship of every institutional controversy. Treat it as internally unequal and increasingly weighty, not a unified revolutionary class. Treat cultural expansion as evidence of resources and public presence, not automatic political radicalization. Preserve this as a contemporary diagnosis and chapter-level synthesis, not proof of inevitable revolution.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Church reform—Jesuit expulsion and suppression of monasteries
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Jesuit expulsion and Brienne’s Commission of Regulars demonstrated the vulnerability of religious corporations to reform and public scrutiny, closing smaller houses and exposing the Church to argument about its institutions. Brienne's role in the Commission of Regulars and later rise from archbishop to chief minister exemplified bishops as reformers, politicians, and powerbrokers. The 1764 Jesuit expulsion exposed Church vulnerability, and the Commission of Regulars dissolved hundreds of small contemplative houses while leaving richer institutions and deeper clerical problems largely untouched. Utilitarian public criticism helped drive selective monastic reform.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Retain the distinct religious reforms and their public reception; agricultural, welfare and parlementary controversies are separate arenas of opinion. Preserve reform activity and openly pursued secular ambition without reducing one to the other. Treat reform as selective and defensive rather than comprehensive renewal.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Parlements combined appellate and administrative jurisdiction with registration of laws, remonstrances, publicity, strikes and resignations. Religious conflicts and especially fiscal demands enlarged opposition and public controversy, provoking Louis XV’s 1766 assertion of undivided sovereignty. As final appellate courts, administrative authorities, and registrars of law, parlements used remonstrances, publicity, strikes, and delay to oppose policy, though the king retained the lit de justice. Religious and especially fiscal conflict expanded provincial parlementary opposition, mobilized public opinion, and provoked Louis XV's 1766 assertion of undivided sovereign power. Printed remonstrances widened parlementary appeals beyond confidential judicial channels. War costs, borrowing and taxation intensified conflict between Crown and parlements; wartime taxes could not readily be reduced.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: These were powerful courts, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Their obstruction and publicity coexisted with the king’s claimed and exercised final power of lit de justice. Treat parlements as powerful courts and political actors, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Preserve both the courts' obstruction and the ultimate legal supremacy claimed and exercised by the monarch.
exact_destination_scopes.scope: Use only this coherent parent’s actual temporal/causal scope; no wholesale replication of a broad historical unit under every destination.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Maupeou reform and restoration of the parlements
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Maupeou exiled resistant magistrates, replaced venal offices and reorganized courts in 1771. Louis XVI reversed the settlement after Louis XV’s death, but restoration recovered neither the parlements’ former credibility nor confidence that monarchy respected legal restraints. Maupeou exiled resisting magistrates, abolished parlementary venality, reorganized subordinate courts, and remodeled provincial parlements but failed to secure public legitimacy before Louis XV died. Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. Louis XV asserted royal sovereignty and supported Maupeou’s judicial reconstruction; his death reopened the settlement. Government propaganda failed during Maupeou’s reform, and expected public confidence influenced restoration.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Preserve the double damage to judicial and royal legitimacy. The predecessor context here concerns judicial policy and succession, not every territorial, military or court episode of the two reigns. Recognize rationalizing elements without accepting official claims or denying the reform's coercive, dispossessing character. Preserve the double damage to both courts and Crown; restoration did not return politics to its earlier state.

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Chronic underemployment, family dependency, population growth, and wages lagging prices left roughly a third of the population poor even in good times. exact_destination_scopes.label: Venal offices and the professional bourgeoisie
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The hereditary resale of public offices made government service a vast capital market and a preferred route from commerce into respectable professional life. Most provincial professionals sought modest hereditary comfort and respectability rather than exceptional fortunes; education, status sensitivity and sociability shaped their lives. Masonic lodges supplied ritual, diversion, ideals and charitable activity within this provincial professional setting. The Crown sold hereditary and transferable public functions, creating more than 70,000 offices that absorbed bourgeois capital and linked finance, administration, status, and law. Most lawyers, notaries, judges, and writers sought modest hereditary comfort rather than great fortunes, filling under-occupied provincial worlds of education and status sensitivity. Masonic lodges offered ideals, ritual, sociability, and charitable activity to educated urban people.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Officeholding provided dignity and modest security more often than great profit, while embedding purchased status throughout the state and judiciary. Masonic participation is a limited sociability and philanthropy route here, not evidence of a revolutionary conspiracy. Treat venality as a central social institution, not merely corruption or a fiscal expedient. Do not generalize exceptional professional success to the group as a whole. The chapter treats masonry as diversion and philanthropy, not a revolutionary conspiracy.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 31–32 support competence, wider recruitment despite noble preference, red/blue officers, maritime classes and naval expansion’s strategic success with unsustainable expense. The complete fiscal-system dossier copied here also imports hospital investment losses, parliamentary conflict, financiers and court expenditure; these are not naval organization or an established specific consequence of naval spending on their cited pages.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 37–38 accurately explain appellate/administrative powers, registration and remonstrance, publicity and obstruction, fiscal confrontation and ultimate royal authority. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Keep the court powers and their fiscal/public-opinion confrontation, explicitly retaining religious and tax triggers in the parent meaning. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 40–41 support financiers’ necessary revenue/credit functions, private enrichment, ennoblement and hostility, including the tax wall’s purpose and symbolic effect. prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Retain finance intermediation and the distinction between indispensable service and public suspicion. Explicitly articulate the wall’s anti-evasion purpose and public interpretation. exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The navy combined more technical professional competence with red and blue officer routes, continuing noble preference, absence of purchased commissions and the classes reserve system for seamen. Expansion helped secure American independence but naval costs and the Cherbourg works added to fiscal exhaustion. Noble naval schools supplied 'red' officers, wartime maritime society supplied 'blues,' and registered naval classes mobilized experienced coastal labor, making competence more important than in the army. Post-1763 naval expansion produced wartime success and helped secure American independence, but sustained fleet and Cherbourg spending contributed to bankruptcy. Naval costs multiplied during the American war, while later defence spending and Cherbourg intensified fiscal strain.

Naval expenditure is a specific fiscal contribution, not the entire monarchy-wide finance dossier. Preserve noble preference without claiming complete noble monopoly or social equality at sea. Preserve both strategic achievement and fiscal unsustainability.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Parlements combined appellate and administrative jurisdiction with registration of laws, remonstrances, publicity, strikes and resignations. Religious conflicts and especially fiscal demands enlarged opposition and public controversy, provoking Louis XV’s 1766 assertion of undivided sovereignty. As final appellate courts, administrative authorities, and registrars of law, parlements used remonstrances, publicity, strikes, and delay to oppose policy, though the king retained the lit de justice. Religious and especially fiscal conflict expanded provincial parlementary opposition, mobilized public opinion, and provoked Louis XV's 1766 assertion of undivided sovereign power. Printed remonstrances widened parlementary appeals beyond confidential judicial channels. War costs, borrowing and taxation intensified conflict between Crown and parlements; wartime taxes could not readily be reduced.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: These were powerful courts, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Their obstruction and publicity coexisted with the king’s claimed and exercised final power of lit de justice. Treat parlements as powerful courts and political actors, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Preserve both the courts' obstruction and the ultimate legal supremacy claimed and exercised by the monarch.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Financiers, tax farming, and public credit
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Financiers, venal financial officeholders and Farmers-General supplied taxation, advances, loans and liquidity essential to royal government while profiting privately from public funds. Inflation, industrial discipline and unrest nevertheless coexisted with master-journeyman solidarity, especially against merchant direction in Lyons. A short-lived attempt to abolish guilds was followed by restoration and a work-record system that tightened employer control over labor mobility. Inflation, regulation, strikes, boycotts, and worker insubordination grew, but shared craft culture often united masters and journeymen against merchants and food-price shocks.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Do not reduce the craft world to a uniform conflict between masters and workers; free trades, exceptional factories and collective craft interests qualified formal regulation. Preserve the reversal from apparent liberalization to renewed regulation. Do not reduce labor relations to a simple master-worker class conflict.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Skilled work—guilds, journeymen and early factories
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Apprenticeship, journeymanship and guild mastership organized skilled work, with small workshops predominant and access to mastership advantaging relatives without being uniformly closed. Illegal compagnonnages aided travelling journeymen with work, solidarity, collective action and sometimes conflict. Larger disciplined, guild-free factories remained exceptional. Training and legal guild organization structured skilled work through apprenticeship, journeymanship, mastership, fees, masterpieces, and craft regulation. Ménétra's tour de France illustrates journeymen's illegal but effective mutual-aid unions, labor organization, mobility, and inter-group violence. Large textile-printing, glass, and wallpaper works introduced exceptional scale, discipline, and guild-free organization into a world of small workshops.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Distinguish master guilds from independent journeyman associations. Hierarchy coexisted with craft solidarity across master-worker divisions, particularly against merchants; factories were exceptions rather than the typical workplace. Avoid depicting guilds as simply closed: access was unequal but often not severely restricted, and mastership did not guarantee success. Treat Ménétra as a sustained illustrative case rather than a principal actor in the chapter. Treat factories as notable exceptions rather than evidence of generalized industrialization.

original_before_fields.label: 'Famine pact' as a conspiracy explanation of grain policy
original_before_fields.meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Repeated shifts between control and liberalization destabilized prices and expectations, while concentration of supply in chosen merchants fueled rumors of a ministerial plot to starve the people. Attempts to restore confidence through preferential contracting instead fostered belief that ministers and a private monopoly were deliberately profiting by starving the people.
original_before_fields.stance: Preserve the combined source qualifications: Report the famine pact as a popular rumor, not an established conspiracy. Record the famine pact as a powerful accusation and belief, not as a demonstrated government conspiracy.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Bourgeoisie—growth, wealth, consumption, and culture
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled commercial, industrial, landed, officeholding and financial wealth. Its demand sustained urban building, luxury trades, education, theatres, print, reading rooms and associations; enrichment alongside growing poverty made inequality more visible. The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled much commercial, industrial, landed, office, and financial wealth, forming most of the secure urban elite. Simultaneous growth of mass poverty and elite wealth made luxury more visible and sharpened resentment between secure elites and precarious majorities. Books, newspapers, reading rooms, clubs and cultural societies expanded the social infrastructure of bourgeois cultural life.

Preserve this as a contemporary diagnosis and chapter-level synthesis, not proof of inevitable revolution.

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The hereditary resale of public offices made government service a vast capital market and a preferred route from commerce into respectable professional life. Most provincial professionals sought modest hereditary comfort and respectability rather than exceptional fortunes; education, status sensitivity and sociability shaped their lives. Masonic lodges supplied ritual, diversion, ideals and charitable activity within this provincial professional setting. The Crown sold hereditary and transferable public functions, creating more than 70,000 offices that absorbed bourgeois capital and linked finance, administration, status, and law. Most lawyers, notaries, judges, and writers sought modest hereditary comfort rather than great fortunes, filling under-occupied provincial worlds of education and status sensitivity. Masonic lodges offered ideals, ritual, sociability, and charitable activity to educated urban people.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Officeholding provided dignity and modest security more often than great profit, while embedding purchased status throughout the state and judiciary. Masonic participation is a limited sociability and philanthropy route here, not evidence of a revolutionary conspiracy. Treat venality as a central social institution, not merely corruption or a fiscal expedient. Do not generalize exceptional professional success to the group as a whole. The chapter treats masonry as diversion and philanthropy, not a revolutionary conspiracy.

original_before_fields.label: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers
original_before_fields.meaning: Professional commoners admired noble status but resented exclusion and moneyed leapfrogging, while pedigree requirements in parlements and the army formalized social barriers.
original_before_fields.stance: Measures such as the Ségur Ordinance appeared to exclude all bourgeois even when aimed at recent wealthy entrants; birth and riches displaced merit.
acceptable_access: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers

independent_basis: Reuse the exact prior inspected meaning/stance and its recorded source-grounded repair disposition, shown below. The current integrated record exactly equals the sealed reviewed value. Historical priority and access are reconciled to the coherent current parent rather than preserved as extra weighted units.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 26–30 sustain resentment, moneyed mobility and public barriers made provocative by converging elite culture. The parent’s focus on formal exclusion and merit captures much of this, but the retained source explicitly also explains substantial permeability and the professional/poor-noble rationale of schools and the Ségur rule. Those qualifications are insufficiently explicit in the parent.
prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Add the permeability of education, marriage, office and wealth, plus the professionalizing/poor-noble aim and courtier loophole, to the parent meaning/stance. Preserve the resulting contradiction rather than framing the rule simply as an attempt to bar the whole bourgeoisie.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Bourgeois-noble relations combined status resentment and barriers to careers with permeability through wealth, education, marriage and office purchase. The Segur Ordinance favoured poor hereditary nobles and professional military standards against rich recent entrants, while court privilege and its appearance of broad bourgeois exclusion complicated that purpose. Education, outlook, marriage, office, and wealth made the bourgeois-noble boundary permeable, yet both professional bourgeois and established nobles defended rank against moneyed parvenus and exclusion. Military schools and the 1781 ancestry requirement aimed to professionalize officers and support poor nobles but preserved privilege, excluded talent, and failed to restrain courtier amateurs.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Distinguish intention, public reception and effects. Established education and social connections could cross order boundaries, while experienced lower-rank officers still faced obstacles; the policy was not simply a uniform ban on the whole bourgeoisie. Reject a rigid caste opposition without minimizing resentment and formal barriers. Preserve the reformers' professional aim and the author's critique of birth and wealth crowding out merit.

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Bourgeois-noble relations combined status resentment and barriers to careers with permeability through wealth, education, marriage and office purchase. exact_destination_scopes.label: Clergy and Church—first estate, wealth, and tax privilege
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The clergy formed the first estate, dominated worship and welfare institutions, owned extensive land and tithes, and defended exemption through representative organization and negotiated contributions. Regular and secular clergy differed in numbers, employment, local presence and resources. The Assembly of Clergy and General Agency managed corporate finance through free gifts and borrowing; parish clergy bore a disproportionate share of the burden. The First Estate included large regular orders, canons, and a minority of parish priests, unevenly distributed; ecclesiastical institutions dominated many townscapes and local economies. The Church held about a tenth of the land, levied uneven tithes, defended ordinary-tax exemption, and used its Assembly, Agency, free gift, internal levies, and credit to negotiate state contributions. Old Regime society distributed rights and exemptions through corporations, towns, provinces, and legally distinct orders, with the nobility and clergy enjoying especially extensive status and fiscal advantages.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Its institutional strength and wealth were real, but uneven distribution within the order left parish clergy carrying disproportionate burdens. Exemption from ordinary taxes did not mean no contribution, and institutional presence varied locally. Do not equate the clergy with parish priests or assume uniform regional presence. Distinguish tax exemption from zero contribution and preserve the low effective burden relative to revenue. Do not reduce privilege to a uniform caste system: exemptions were widespread, varied by place and body, and coexisted with substantial mobility into nobility.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Third estate as nation and attack on privilege
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Third-estate spokesmen increasingly equated the nation with associates under common law and attacked privilege as exclusion from equal representation and careers. Fiscal equality commanded wider assent than civil or political equality; opponents defended privilege as property. Educated propertied leaders’ programme differed from popular livelihood demands, while criticism of clerical privilege did not mean every parish reformer abandoned Catholic authority. The earlier consensus against despotism broke apart when representation was recast as a struggle between the productive nation and privileged orders. Educated commoners recognized a durable public role and organized to make the third estate politically dominant. Privilege moved from a defended corporate right and fiscal exception to a general indictment of unequal law and political exclusion. Third-estate claims increasingly appropriated the language of nation and patriotism, displacing its earlier focus on resistance to despotism. Renunciation of order-based tax exemptions commanded broader agreement than political equality or common voting. Third-estate deputies joined tax equality to a commitment to equal civil status and opposition to corporate legal privilege. Clergy became targets of anti-privilege publicity, crowd suspicion, and attacks associated with hoarding and sacrilege. Fiscal equality could be accepted while order-based political representation was defended.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Preserve Sieyes’s mobilizing logic and the source’s correction that privilege extended beyond nobles and clergy. Class limits, property-based arguments and deeper clerical solidarity qualify any simple unified anti-privilege bloc. The chapter explicitly marks this repolarization as rapid, mutually reinforcing, and central to the failure of compromise. The author treats bourgeois mobilization as politically transformative while distinguishing its leaders from poorer urban and rural populations. The source preserves competing meanings: defenders linked privilege to property and order, while anti-privilege writers made its incompatibility with national common law decisive. The chapter presents this semantic change as both a source of unity for commoners and an exclusionary pressure on compromise. The chapter repeatedly distinguishes fiscal equality from surrender of political, social, feudal, and corporate privilege. The chapter treats civil equality as a central common commitment, distinct from the narrower fiscal concession many privileged deputies accepted. The author distinguishes hostility to clerical privilege and institutions from the more complex political behavior of parish-priest deputies.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Clergy and Church—first estate, wealth, and tax privilege
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The clergy formed the first estate, dominated worship and welfare institutions, owned extensive land and tithes, and defended exemption through representative organization and negotiated contributions. Regular and secular clergy differed in numbers, employment, local presence and resources. The Assembly of Clergy and General Agency managed corporate finance through free gifts and borrowing; parish clergy bore a disproportionate share of the burden. The First Estate included large regular orders, canons, and a minority of parish priests, unevenly distributed; ecclesiastical institutions dominated many townscapes and local economies. The Church held about a tenth of the land, levied uneven tithes, defended ordinary-tax exemption, and used its Assembly, Agency, free gift, internal levies, and credit to negotiate state contributions. Old Regime society distributed rights and exemptions through corporations, towns, provinces, and legally distinct orders, with the nobility and clergy enjoying especially extensive status and fiscal advantages.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Its institutional strength and wealth were real, but uneven distribution within the order left parish clergy carrying disproportionate burdens. Exemption from ordinary taxes did not mean no contribution, and institutional presence varied locally. Do not equate the clergy with parish priests or assume uniform regional presence. Distinguish tax exemption from zero contribution and preserve the low effective burden relative to revenue. Do not reduce privilege to a uniform caste system: exemptions were widespread, varied by place and body, and coexisted with substantial mobility into nobility.

The Assembly of Clergy and General Agency managed corporate finance through free gifts and borrowing; parish clergy bore a disproportionate share of the burden. The First Estate included large regular orders, canons, and a minority of parish priests, unevenly distributed; ecclesiastical institutions dominated many townscapes and local economies. The Church held about a tenth of the land, levied uneven tithes, defended ordinary-tax exemption, and used its Assembly, Agency, free gift, internal levies, and credit to negotiate state contributions. Old Regime society distributed rights and exemptions through corporations, towns, provinces, and legally distinct orders, with the nobility and clergy enjoying especially extensive status and fiscal advantages.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Its institutional strength and wealth were real, but uneven distribution within the order left parish clergy carrying disproportionate burdens. Exemption from ordinary taxes did not mean no contribution, and institutional presence varied locally. Do not equate the clergy with parish priests or assume uniform regional presence. Distinguish tax exemption from zero contribution and preserve the low effective burden relative to revenue. Do not reduce privilege to a uniform caste system: exemptions were widespread, varied by place and body, and coexisted with substantial mobility into nobility.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Parlements combined appellate and administrative jurisdiction with registration of laws, remonstrances, publicity, strikes and resignations. Religious conflicts and especially fiscal demands enlarged opposition and public controversy, provoking Louis XV’s 1766 assertion of undivided sovereignty. As final appellate courts, administrative authorities, and registrars of law, parlements used remonstrances, publicity, strikes, and delay to oppose policy, though the king retained the lit de justice. Religious and especially fiscal conflict expanded provincial parlementary opposition, mobilized public opinion, and provoked Louis XV's 1766 assertion of undivided sovereign power. Printed remonstrances widened parlementary appeals beyond confidential judicial channels. War costs, borrowing and taxation intensified conflict between Crown and parlements; wartime taxes could not readily be reduced.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: These were powerful courts, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Their obstruction and publicity coexisted with the king’s claimed and exercised final power of lit de justice. Treat parlements as powerful courts and political actors, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Preserve both the courts' obstruction and the ultimate legal supremacy claimed and exercised by the monarch.

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Maupeou exiled resistant magistrates, replaced venal offices and reorganized courts in 1771. exact_destination_scopes.label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. Louis XV had failed to prepare his heir; the young queen and court appointment pressures formed the immediate setting of the new reign. The twenty-year-old king was educated, devout, dutiful, and well-intentioned but poorly prepared, insecure, unimpressive, and unlikely to master the intrigue surrounding the throne. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV failed to prepare his heir for kingship; this shaped the personal inheritance at accession. Louis XVI’s indecisive accession contrasted with Louis XIV’s decisive assumption of authority.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Credit conscientious intentions while retaining political insecurity. Early marital and court tensions do not establish later revolutionary accusations; territorial conquest and army history belong to their own requirements. Avoid caricature: credit good intentions and duty while preserving the author's judgment of inadequate political mastery. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. exact_destination_scopes.label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. original_before_fields.label: French cultural prestige and language in eighteenth-century Europe
original_before_fields.meaning: The legacy of Versailles and French court culture made French architecture, fashions, material culture, and especially the French language dominant markers of elite cultivation across much of Europe.
original_before_fields.stance: French cultural predominance remained powerful into the 1770s, despite a still-limited backlash against imitation of an alien culture.

independent_basis: The wording change around 1770s is typographic; the repaired main parent also states the source’s linguistic transmission mechanism. German/Italian backlash remains a limited countercurrent rather than a claim that French prestige had already collapsed.

prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.basis: Pages 44–45 sustain French courtly/cultural prestige and limited German/Italian backlash. The retained language distinction also makes French a practical vehicle for foreign readers to follow events, form judgments and receive ideas. The parent meaning casts language primarily as an elite cultural marker, leaving that transmission mechanism unstated.
prior_source_grounded_parent_judgments.proposed_fix: Add the shared language’s role in transnational political observation and print circulation. Preserve continuing dominance alongside the limited countercurrent; major priority remains suitable.

exact_destination_scopes.label: French cultural prestige and language in eighteenth-century Europe
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The legacy of Versailles and French court culture made French architecture, fashions, material culture, and especially the French language dominant markers of elite cultivation across much of Europe. A shared elite language made French political developments and printed debate accessible across Europe, multiplying transnational observation. Louis XIV's court, palace, gardens, architecture, furnishings, and fashions established a model copied by rulers and elites across eighteenth-century Europe. French became the preferred language of courts and cultivated society across much of Europe, enabling educated readers to follow French affairs and consume French print directly. By the 1770 s writers in Germany and Italy attacked their compatriots' deference to French language and culture, although the reaction remained limited.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: French cultural predominance remained powerful into the 1770 s, despite a still-limited backlash against imitation of an alien culture. Nascent nationalist resistance had not yet displaced French cultural and linguistic dominance. Treat cultural prestige as a durable political legacy of Louis XIV, not as proof that French dominance was uncontested or permanent. Preserve both the breadth of francophone culture and the chapter's link between linguistic access, informed judgment, and the spread of French ideas. Do not imply that backlash had already displaced French prestige; it marks an emerging countercurrent.

exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The legacy of Versailles and French court culture made French architecture, fashions, material culture, and especially the French language dominant markers of elite cultivation across much of Europe. A shared elite language made French political developments and printed debate accessible across Europe, multiplying transnational observation. Louis XIV's court, palace, gardens, architecture, furnishings, and fashions established a model copied by rulers and elites across eighteenth-century Europe. French became the preferred language of courts and cultivated society across much of Europe, enabling educated readers to follow French affairs and consume French print directly. By the 1770 s writers in Germany and Italy attacked their compatriots' deference to French language and culture, although the reaction remained limited.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: French cultural predominance remained powerful into the 1770 s, despite a still-limited backlash against imitation of an alien culture. Nascent nationalist resistance had not yet displaced French cultural and linguistic dominance. Treat cultural prestige as a durable political legacy of Louis XIV, not as proof that French dominance was uncontested or permanent. Preserve both the breadth of francophone culture and the chapter's link between linguistic access, informed judgment, and the spread of French ideas. Do not imply that backlash had already displaced French prestige; it marks an emerging countercurrent.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Expansion of the French-language periodical press
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The French-language press expanded through semi-official newspapers, independent journals, clandestine Jansenist publication, foreign presses and local or daily papers. Linguet sustained oppositional journalism through imprisonment and publication beyond royal jurisdiction; his memoirs shaped the Bastille’s reputation. Foreign journals supplied informed opposition as well as conservative and radical outlooks. The number and variety of journals rose sharply during the eighteenth century, widening access to political, religious, learned, literary, and general news. Semi-official journals remained closely censored, but the multiplying press exceeded the government's capacity for comprehensive supervision. The Jansenist Nouvelles ecclésiastiques maintained a sustained critique of the established Church while repeatedly evading efforts to locate and suppress its presses. Linguet's Annales survived his imprisonment through surrogates, popularized his attack on arbitrary detention, and later operated from the Austrian Netherlands to escape French control. French-language journals printed in Holland, Avignon, Prussian territories, and independent Bouillon supplied detailed reporting and intellectual criticism beyond ordinary French jurisdiction. Political upheavals increased demand for news; foreign and domestic circulation rose, provincial centers acquired papers, and a daily Paris press reached an audience far larger than copy totals alone.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Retain distinct channels, continuing selective repression and estimated readership. Extraterritorial publication was not uniformly radical, and imprisonment did not necessarily silence a journal. Treat expansion as a structural enlargement of the informed public, while retaining the fragility of many individual journals. Avoid portraying censorship as absent; the point is declining practical control amid continued legal authority and selective repression. Treat the journal as an organized political-religious intervention, not merely as a title in a list of periodicals. Preserve his unpredictability and personal notoriety; do not turn him into a consistent revolutionary ideologue. Do not equate all foreign journals with radicalism; their outlooks ranged from conservative to anticlerical and anti-authoritarian. Treat the reported readership as an estimate and the press as expanding, not universally accessible.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Expansion of the French-language periodical press
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The French-language press expanded through semi-official newspapers, independent journals, clandestine Jansenist publication, foreign presses and local or daily papers. Linguet sustained oppositional journalism through imprisonment and publication beyond royal jurisdiction; his memoirs shaped the Bastille’s reputation. Foreign journals supplied informed opposition as well as conservative and radical outlooks. The number and variety of journals rose sharply during the eighteenth century, widening access to political, religious, learned, literary, and general news. Semi-official journals remained closely censored, but the multiplying press exceeded the government's capacity for comprehensive supervision. The Jansenist Nouvelles ecclésiastiques maintained a sustained critique of the established Church while repeatedly evading efforts to locate and suppress its presses. Linguet's Annales survived his imprisonment through surrogates, popularized his attack on arbitrary detention, and later operated from the Austrian Netherlands to escape French control. French-language journals printed in Holland, Avignon, Prussian territories, and independent Bouillon supplied detailed reporting and intellectual criticism beyond ordinary French jurisdiction. Political upheavals increased demand for news; foreign and domestic circulation rose, provincial centers acquired papers, and a daily Paris press reached an audience far larger than copy totals alone.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Retain distinct channels, continuing selective repression and estimated readership. Extraterritorial publication was not uniformly radical, and imprisonment did not necessarily silence a journal. Treat expansion as a structural enlargement of the informed public, while retaining the fragility of many individual journals. Avoid portraying censorship as absent; the point is declining practical control amid continued legal authority and selective repression. Treat the journal as an organized political-religious intervention, not merely as a title in a list of periodicals. Preserve his unpredictability and personal notoriety; do not turn him into a consistent revolutionary ideologue. Do not equate all foreign journals with radicalism; their outlooks ranged from conservative to anticlerical and anti-authoritarian. Treat the reported readership as an estimate and the press as expanding, not universally accessible.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Literacy, reading access, and the social composition of the reading public
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Rising literacy and shared-reading institutions widened access to print, but cost and education meant that the cultivated reading public was still dominated by urban nobles, clergy, and professional bourgeois groups. Basic literacy opened access to cheap traditional blue-library print but did not make sophisticated books and journals affordable. Subscription libraries, reading rooms and other fee-based institutions widened access unevenly; noble, clerical and professional readers outweighed merchants in cultivated readership. More than a third of the population could read and write, sustaining a market for cheap almanacs and traditional tales distributed by traveling hawkers. Journal subscriptions and books cost too much for most artisans, and even comfortable readers needed collective institutions to sustain broad access to current literature. Provincial subscription libraries and reading rooms lowered the cost of following literature and political news and sometimes added spaces for conversation. Readers of sophisticated print were chiefly nobles, clergy, lawyers, magistrates, administrators, officers, and other professional bourgeois, concentrated in towns and less strongly represented among merchants and manufacturers.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Access broadened beyond individual purchasers without becoming socially democratic; merchants and manufacturers were comparatively less engaged than professional and administrative readers. Do not infer broad access to sophisticated Enlightenment print from basic literacy or popular-book consumption. Treat economic exclusion as a central limit on the numerical reach of enlightened opinion. Do not describe these institutions as socially universal; fees still selected a comparatively prosperous reading public. Avoid treating the bourgeoisie as a single uniformly enlightened class; occupation, education, residence, and disposable income mattered.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Education after the suppression of the Jesuits
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: The expulsion and dissolution of the Jesuits fragmented French elite education, while colleges retained classical and Catholic foundations but increasingly taught scientific and experimental approaches. Experimental and Newtonian instruction could supply habits of rational criticism and practical usefulness later applied to human institutions. The expulsion and dissolution of the Jesuits broke the uniformity of Catholic elite education, dispersed their colleges among varied successors, and left France without a kingdom-wide replacement system. Elite secondary education still centered on years of Latin and Roman culture, reinforced by Catholic orthodoxy, with only limited additions such as geography and French history. Advanced college courses spread the methods and findings of the scientific revolution, including Newtonian physics, behind a formally Aristotelian facade. Students trained to judge nature by demonstrable operation and useful results could extend the same standards to social and political institutions despite lessons in obedience and orthodoxy. Classical and Catholic curricula persisted alongside newer scientific instruction.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Institutional disruption produced diversity rather than a coordinated national reform; Newtonian and empirical teaching coexisted with formal Aristotelian and religious orthodoxy. This was a possible intellectual pathway, not proof that every scientifically educated pupil became a reformer; classical and Catholic education persisted. Do not equate institutional disruption with educational collapse; the result was greater diversity, not simple disappearance. Do not portray the curriculum as wholly secularized or modernized before the Revolution. Preserve the coexistence of institutional tradition and substantive intellectual change. Treat this as an interpretive pathway and intellectual possibility, not a deterministic claim that scientific education made every student a reformer.

exact_destination_scopes.label: The Enlightenment as a program of rational criticism and practical improvement
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Enlightenment writers addressed an unprecedentedly literate educated public with criticism, popularization, and claims that institutions should be judged by reason, usefulness, and human happiness. Shared persecution and common adversaries helped create a collective philosophic identity without doctrinal uniformity. The Enlightenment is defined as a movement of criticism that subjected institutions and beliefs to rational tests of improvement, usefulness, and contribution to human happiness. Enlightenment writers styled themselves independent thinkers committed to practical improvement and sought influence through polemic, simplification, and appeal to the educated public. Harassment by the Church and clerically influenced authorities helped disparate speculative writers recognize a shared movement and common cause. Mainstream enlightened thought treated material and intellectual progress as a winning struggle against superstition and as a force improving human welfare and institutions.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The movement is presented as reformist, public-facing, and practically oriented rather than merely speculative, while containing internal disagreements and orthodoxies of its own. Progress and improvement were optimistic expectations contested within enlightened culture, not demonstrated universal laws. Preserve the movement's reformist and practical orientation without reducing its diversity to one doctrine. Do not confuse their activist self-conception with the older ideal of detached philosophical contemplation. Do not imply complete doctrinal unity; solidarity arose partly from common enemies and experiences of repression. Preserve the movement's optimism while noting shocks such as the Lisbon earthquake and the existence of dissenting positions.

Experimental and Newtonian instruction could supply habits of rational criticism and practical usefulness later applied to human institutions. The expulsion and dissolution of the Jesuits broke the uniformity of Catholic elite education, dispersed their colleges among varied successors, and left France without a kingdom-wide replacement system. Elite secondary education still centered on years of Latin and Roman culture, reinforced by Catholic orthodoxy, with only limited additions such as geography and French history. Advanced college courses spread the methods and findings of the scientific revolution, including Newtonian physics, behind a formally Aristotelian facade. Students trained to judge nature by demonstrable operation and useful results could extend the same standards to social and political institutions despite lessons in obedience and orthodoxy. Classical and Catholic curricula persisted alongside newer scientific instruction.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Institutional disruption produced diversity rather than a coordinated national reform; Newtonian and empirical teaching coexisted with formal Aristotelian and religious orthodoxy. This was a possible intellectual pathway, not proof that every scientifically educated pupil became a reformer; classical and Catholic education persisted. Do not equate institutional disruption with educational collapse; the result was greater diversity, not simple disappearance. Do not portray the curriculum as wholly secularized or modernized before the Revolution. Preserve the coexistence of institutional tradition and substantive intellectual change. Treat this as an interpretive pathway and intellectual possibility, not a deterministic claim that scientific education made every student a reformer.

exact_destination_scopes.label: The Enlightenment as a program of rational criticism and practical improvement
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Enlightenment writers addressed an unprecedentedly literate educated public with criticism, popularization, and claims that institutions should be judged by reason, usefulness, and human happiness. Shared persecution and common adversaries helped create a collective philosophic identity without doctrinal uniformity. The Enlightenment is defined as a movement of criticism that subjected institutions and beliefs to rational tests of improvement, usefulness, and contribution to human happiness. Enlightenment writers styled themselves independent thinkers committed to practical improvement and sought influence through polemic, simplification, and appeal to the educated public. Harassment by the Church and clerically influenced authorities helped disparate speculative writers recognize a shared movement and common cause. Mainstream enlightened thought treated material and intellectual progress as a winning struggle against superstition and as a force improving human welfare and institutions.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: The movement is presented as reformist, public-facing, and practically oriented rather than merely speculative, while containing internal disagreements and orthodoxies of its own. Progress and improvement were optimistic expectations contested within enlightened culture, not demonstrated universal laws. Preserve the movement's reformist and practical orientation without reducing its diversity to one doctrine. Do not confuse their activist self-conception with the older ideal of detached philosophical contemplation. Do not imply complete doctrinal unity; solidarity arose partly from common enemies and experiences of repression. Preserve the movement's optimism while noting shocks such as the Lisbon earthquake and the existence of dissenting positions.

exact_destination_scopes.label: The Encyclopédie and encyclopedism
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Diderot and D'Alembert's Encyclopédie sought both to organize knowledge and to cultivate critical reflection, becoming a contested, widely distributed vehicle of independent thought. Malesherbes’s administrative protection helped the project survive repression. Diderot’s later radical thought extended beyond the early collective enterprise and beyond what contemporary readers knew of him. Diderot and D'Alembert transformed a translated reference project into a multi-author work intended both to organize knowledge and cultivate critical, philosophic reflection. Repeated attacks and suspension culminated in withdrawal of the Encyclopédie's privilege, but Malesherbes allowed publication to continue under tacit permission until completion. Expanded editions and smaller formats created a large market; notoriety, irreverence, and contempt for authority made the work influential, while encyclopedism came to signify independent judgment. Disillusioned with the Encyclopédie, Diderot moved toward political and economic radicalism while habits formed under censorship kept much of that development obscured from contemporaries.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Censorship and notoriety enlarged its influence; its anti-authoritarian ethos was historically important, though encyclopedism also carried a confident orthodoxy of progress. Distinguish the project’s contemporary reputation from Diderot’s later or unpublished positions; censorship also generated publicity. Do not reduce the Encyclopédie either to a neutral reference work or to a simple revolutionary manifesto. Preserve the unstable combination of official repression, administrative protection, and continued production. Recognize both the work's reference quality and the anti-authoritarian reputation that chiefly drove sales. Do not infer that his public reputation in 1784 matched his later-recognized radical importance.

exact_destination_scopes.label: Rousseau's critique of progress, natural goodness, and legitimate authority
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_meaning: Rousseau argued that institutions and material progress could corrupt natural goodness. His novels and educational writing cultivated feeling and individual virtue, while the Social Contract theorized legitimate authority for small communities through a general will distinct from numerical majority. Later readers converted its formulas into a model of national regeneration. Rousseau rejected the orthodox claim that arts and sciences improved humanity, arguing instead that social institutions corrupted people who were naturally good. Julie and Émile used an emotionally direct style to dramatize innocence and virtue preserved against the corrupting snares of established society, winning a vast European readership. Rousseau's Social Contract offered a theoretical account of legitimate political authority compatible with natural liberty and warned that its model could function only in small city-states. Rousseau's infallible general will was not necessarily majority opinion, but common usage quickly simplified it into majority will and later revolutionaries treated it as part of a program for national regeneration. The religious passages of the Social Contract and Émile criticized clerical Christianity and affirmed a benevolent natural deity, provoking condemnation, an arrest decree, and exile.
exact_destination_scopes.current_main_stance: Literary morality is not a direct programme for wholesale social revolution. Civil and natural religion, including the Savoyard curate, prompted condemnation; Rousseau’s natural deity and criticism of clerical religion were not atheism. Treat his position as a foundational dissent within the Enlightenment, not as simple rejection of reason or all reform. Do not collapse these works into a political program; their primary treatment here concerns moral sentiment and social corruption. Do not present the work as a direct blueprint for wholesale French revolution or a program designed for a large monarchy. Preserve the distinction between Rousseau's qualified concept and its later political simplification. Preserve Rousseau's emotional religiosity; he appeared blasphemous to the devout but was not simply an atheist.
